However, because the Prosecutor has accepted the authenticity of a number of documents, we waived the right to call four witnesses. Mira Busalic was also on the list of our witnesses. Because of a surgery that she is going to have in Konjic, she couldn't come, so we are submitting her written statement. Therefore, we will be calling six witnesses. Before I call the first witness, since the Prosecutor has agreed as to the authenticity of the documents, I would kindly ask that the originals of these documents be made part of the record, that they be marked for identification, and I'm tendering them into evidence. I would now kindly ask the assistance of the usher and the registrar so that the evidence --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I believe there's a problem, Your Honour, because it may be that we have agreed to this, but we were shown some documents this morning. Maybe I could just see them before they are tendered so that I can check them out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not referring to any piece of evidence that you saw this morning. I'm going to hand in every original of this material. The first one is the information regarding the criminal record of Zejnil Delalic in Germany, that is, that he has no criminal record in Germany. Then the next piece is the same type of document from Konjic, Bosnia and Herzegovina. Then there is a document from Vienna testifying to his involvement and engagement in sports. Then there's a document from Vienna speaking about his humanitarian efforts, and also a document from Konjic dated the 5th of October, 1998 that was compiled for the purposes of the International Tribunal. This is part of our written submission, and the Prosecutor has stated his position about these documents on the first day of the trial. I would now kindly ask that these documents be tendered into evidence, of course, that they be first marked for identification. I kindly ask the Court to accept these documents as evidence in this case. Could you please tell me the numbers for the purpose of identification and also the numbers for the purpose of admission?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have these documents been admitted by the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann just wanted to have a look at these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Pass them on to the Prosecution so that they can see what they are admitting. I hear it is being admitted by concession, by agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I thought that Ms. McHenry had confirmed that these are the documents which are part of the written submission and in respect of which she has already stated her position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I have no objection to this document, Your Honour, which is 191/1. I have no objection to 192/1, Your Honour. I have no objection to 193/1, Your Honour. I have no objection to 194/1, Your Honour. I have no objection to 195/1. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are these documents, therefore, admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I now proceed with my first witness, Alija Buturovic?

utterances.speaker: THE USHER
utterances.text: Please remain standing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly swear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE USHER
utterances.text: Could you read this out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may take your seat, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I begin, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Buturovic.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please introduce yourself by stating your full name and surname to this honourable Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: My name is Alija Buturovic. I was born on the 17th of September, 1946 in Sejenice in the municipality of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak Muslim by nationality, and I'm a national of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is your occupation? I'm a teacher of geography, and currently I'm the head of an institution that is involved with public work in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. The witness's answer was "I'm a Bosniak Muslim ..." and for the clarity in the transcript, it's written as a question, when that was his an answer. That's on line 24 of page 59 of the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I see it, but I don't see the need for the question mark. The rest of what he said has been transcribed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, do you know Zejnil Delalic, and if you do, for how long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I have known Mr. Zejnil Delalic since my youth, since I was 16, when we went to grammar school together. We spent four years in school together.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, do you know where Mr. Zejnil Delalic lived at the time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Zejnil Delalic was born and he lived in the town of Ostrozac which is situated some 12 kilometres south of Konjic. He lived in a large worker's family, and every day he commuted to school by train. I come from a peasant family myself, and I also come from a large family, from a village not far from his. So we come from similar families that had to struggle rather hard for life.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you say, Mr. Buturovic, that you come from a large family, what exactly do you mean? How many children were there in the family of Mr. Zejnil Delalic; do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I know for sure that the family had at least nine members. As far as I know, there were nine of them, maybe more.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the family was poor. Do you know whether, at that time, at the age of 15 or 17, whether Zejnil Delalic had to work for his education?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I remember Mr. Zejnil Delalic as a secondary school student, and I know he couldn't buy books for the school. Very often, we did really hard, physical work in order to make some money because of the situation. We would cut firewood, clean streets in the winter, distribute all kinds of groceries to families who were better off. This was the main source of income for Mr. Zejnil Delalic and myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You stated that Zejnil Delalic had to travel to school by train and go back to his village and had to do hard, physical work. What kind of student was he at school?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I remember very well that Zejnil Delalic was a very good student, and he was especially gifted in humanities, history, for example, in particular, geography, foreign languages, literature. I remember that he was in charge of the literary section, literary group, that functioned within the grammar school.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, after you completed your secondary education in Konjic, did you continue meeting Zejnil Delalic and socialising with him? If you did, could you tell us when and where?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: After I finished high school, I enrolled in the studies at the Pedagogical Academy in Sarajevo, and Mr. Zejnil Delalic became a student of the Faculty of Philosophy in Sarajevo. That happened in the same year that we completed our secondary education.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did Zejnil Delalic have to work to provide money for his university education?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The problems were even greater at that time. At that time, we were both members of the so-called student service in Sarajevo, which is a large university city. It has a large student population. We had to look for various jobs in order to make some money. Again, we were doing very hard, physical labour. We were working at various construction sites. We had to carry construction material, cut firewood, again, various types of physical services that we had to do all the time, including weekends.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buturovic. Was there a period of time when you did not see each other. If so, could you tell us why that occurred?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: After I completed my studies at the teacher's academy, I went to Prozor to work at the local school. Prozor is about 45 kilometres away from Sarajevo. After he graduated from the Faculty of Philosophy, Zejnil went abroad. At that moment, we, obviously, stopped seeing each other. I soon learned that he became involved in business and that he was quite successful at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, we have here a poor, young man who had to work to provide for his own education, a young man who eventually became a very successful professional person. Tell us, is Zejnil Delalic the kind of person who forgot his friends and his country when he became successful?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: The break in our contact was not very long, and Mr. Delalic, very often when he was on leave, on vacation, he would come to his home country. He would visit his home municipality, and we would get together. We would often remember our childhood, our university days. Even these brief encounters were enough for me to realise that Mr. Delalic was the kind of person who was ready to help his friends, to help the local institutions, in all areas of social life, culture, arts, social work, and so on. He was very honest, very sincere about that. He was really ready to help his friends and his hometown in general.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During his youth, was Zejnil Delalic a sociable man? Did he enjoy the company of other people?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: He was very liked in the secondary school and at the university. Later on, when he would come for leave from abroad, he would always express his readiness to help, to assist people in various things. He was very sociable, and he always liked to help his friends in trouble. He would always manage to find some reasonable and practical solution. In our generation, the background of a person was not important, I mean, his religious or ethnic background.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have described Mr. Delalic as a sociable man. Did he have respect for all these people, for all the people he socialised with, or did he try to impose on them his opinions?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: While contacting his friends and his business partners, he would always treat people equally. He never tried to establish himself as some kind of leader. Of course, he had his opinion and his stance about many things, and that was only natural, but he was ready to listen to the opinion of others as well. Finally, he would always come up with an acceptable solution for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buturovic. Let us go back to something that you've mentioned. He said that he wanted to help both his friends, his family, and his former environment, in general. Do you know of any specific example which illustrates that Zejnil Delalic, who was a successful businessman working abroad, that he also helped his hometown and his friends?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, his hometown, Ostrozac, which is situated in a beautiful countryside, managed to get a club, a sports club on that lake. This is something that Zejnil Delalic helped with. He organised that kind of work, and he managed to organise the establishment of other sports clubs in the area. Unfortunately, because of the aggression in Bosnia and Herzegovina, this was not carried out to the end. At that time, Konjic was known as a small and peaceful town, which had a very intense cultural life, namely, the so-called Neretva Cultural and Arts Society. It had a very successful acting group which performed throughout Yugoslavia and even abroad. There was also a very successful choir called Djevojkes Neretva, which was lead by a Russia singer, and that choir travelled a lot throughout Europe. When it came to providing necessary equipment and necessary funds for these types of societies, it was Zejnil Delalic who helped do that, either personally, directly, or through his friends and business relations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, you said that you were headmaster of a school. Did Zejnil Delalic ever help your school to upgrade the level of education for the students of that particular school?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked as the headmaster of an elementary school which, according to our legislation, was responsible for primary education. It was a very poor village, very poor little town in the area. The school had about 800 students, and it was very poorly equipped. It did not have a very good library and other necessary equipment. When he came on one occasion, I believe it was in 1982, he asked me whether there was anything he could do for my school, and I said that there were quite a few things that could be done. He wrote a cheque for me, and the amount, as I remember it, was something around 8.000 German marks. We used that money to buy books for our library and to buy other necessary equipment, including overhead projectors and other teaching aids. We bought a number of very good pieces of technical equipment, and thanks to this technical support, our school received numerous awards. It received the highest award in Bosnia and Herzegovina that was given at the time. It is an award called Hasim Verkic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, the Court is already familiar with the fact that both Konjic and Jablanica are towns with mixed populations, as is often the case with the majority of towns in Bosnia and Herzegovina. You come from a poor area. There are not very good roads in your area, not many tarmac roads. Zejnil Delalic, through his involvement, did he try to help the quality of life of all people, regardless of their national and religious backgrounds? Do you know of any specific example in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that it is a very wide geographical area, some 300 square kilometres, with approximately 8.000 inhabitants. It is very poorly connected with the rest of the country. At that time, we had a so-called self-contribution. That was something that the citizens had to vote for and sign. We organised a self-contribution referendum to build a road. Mr. Delalic influenced that activity, that action, and it was thanks to him that the work was finally completed. I know of a number of other examples where he helped, not only financially but in other ways as well, a number of schools, public institutions, and individual persons as well. The people in that area, most of them are farmers, and there are not many people who are employed in factories and other institutions. I know that thanks to Mr. Zejnil Delalic, a number of people managed to find work abroad in Western Europe, and some of them are still there living quite comfortable lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When helping his neighbours and their families from these impoverished areas, did Zejnil distinguish between ethnic or religious groups as to whom he would help to come abroad and help their families back home?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I still have very close ties with this area, professionally speaking. I know that there were several large Croatian families whom he helped go to Austria or Germany. I know Sveto Zuza who is a Serb and a mason. Through Zejnil's help, he was able to go abroad. Then the families Pozder, Begic, Sokolovic, Sutlic, in other words, this tells you that he did not distinguish between Serbs and Muslims and Croats in a sense of whom he was going to help.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This question regards your acquaintance with Mr. Delalic before the war and while he was a young man. I would like to ask you now, Mr. Buturovic, what you did at the time when the war broke out, and, if you know, where was Mr. Zejnil Delalic at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: In 1986, I was appointed director of the Centre for Social Affairs in Konjic. It was a municipal agency. I was in that duty in 1991 and 1992 when the war broke out, first in Croatia and then in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that on the eve of the war, Zejnil's brother Rasim died, and do you know that Zejnil came to Konjic at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was at the dzenaza of the deceased brother, and I was present there in Konjic, and I know that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you said that you were the director of the Centre for Social Affairs, you were forced to handle a large number of refugees which flooded, first, the area of Konjic municipality and then the town of Konjic itself. Can you tell us a little bit about that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: The war in Croatia in 1991 did affect my municipality as well. In 1991, there were a significant number of refugees, mostly from Eastern Slavonia, Tenje, Borovo Naselje, and Vukovar. Those were refugees of both Serbian and Croatian background, and I was appointed the chief of the Municipal Staff for refugees who came flooding from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, did our own population come to Konjic? Did you talk to Zejnil about this, and what was his position towards that issue?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: In early April 1992, the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina started, and it also broke out in my municipality. During that period, I occasionally saw Mr. Delalic. These were very short meetings. I continued to work with my team which had been appointed. There were still Croatian and Serb refugees from Eastern Slavonia. In early April, refugees from Eastern Herzegovina started appearing in Konjic. When the shelling of Konjic started, that was around 4 May, 1992, a large number of inhabitants of the villages around Konjic came to town fleeing from the aggressor and the destruction, torture, and mistreatment that accompanied this attack, so that thousands of refugees flooded into the town proper at the beginning of this war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Court is familiar with some of these events, but I would like you to focus on where these refugees were accommodated. Did Zejnil Delalic help in this, or did you ask for any advice and any assistance from him?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Since order broke down in town and chaos ensued, the population was not ready for these events, and the body to which I was assigned to deal with refugees was trying to accommodate them as much as possible, to provide them with food and shelter. As we were not well prepared for this, we initially would accommodate them in school buildings, in basements of residential buildings, and in factories and workers's dormitories. Through the president of the War Presidency and the Economic Affairs officer, plus the Caritas and Merhamet organisations, I sought any help I could get. Zejnil Delalic provided advice. He provided advice as to the best accommodation for these people, because at that time, hundreds of shells were falling on Konjic. While receiving these first waves of refugees, he first provided his own tea and canned food from his personal stocks, as well as medicine for children.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, in these first days of war, in June, for instance, when there was not enough school space or basement space, did Zejnil Delalic offer his own property, his own house, for the accommodation of refugees until your committee found the right accommodation for them?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Since this committee was not prepared for this, and there were many civilian casualties of war, the health centre, which then became a war hospital and which, today, is the municipal hospital, was filled with the injured and the sick. Mr. Delalic offered the basement of his house, and my subordinate, a colleague of mine, went there on several occasions and brought back some things that were needed. In the basement of his house, occasionally, there were 10 to 15 people from, let's say, Focaka, Gacana, or Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This may be a good moment for a break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will reassemble at 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.03 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while they are getting the witness, I have two housekeeping matters. One, Mr. Karabdic is currently detained somewhere else and he will be here in a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I didn't understand what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I have two housekeeping matters while they are getting the witness. The first is Mr. Karabdic is detained taking a statement from Mrs. Delic, and he shall be here in a few minutes, probably. The other is that Mr. Delic's wife, of course, is in town, and that's a fairly rare event. He asked to be excused tomorrow so that he can visit his wife. The Prosecutor has no objection to it. Of course, I will be here to represent his interests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose so. Yes, he could be excused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: I have one question. Have you determined how long we can have in closing arguments? My question was, have you determined how long we will have to argue the close, tomorrow or the next day, whenever that comes. In the scheduling order, it said you would entertain brief closing arguments. I have an idea of what I think that means, and I just want to compare it to what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't think we're regarding them as arguments, but brief submissions to argue what you have done. I thought that your submission should not be more than a few minutes for each closing submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Is 15 minutes too long?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Too long for any --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: That's fine. I'm writing it, so if I just write five minutes worth, rather than fifteen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You have already written what you want to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While we are discussing times, Your Honour, I thought I might raise our position. We, of course, put in our submission first and have never had an opportunity to respond to the Defence's submissions which were given in writing. So we will take longer than 15 minutes. I don't think it would take much longer than about an hour, but it would take about that long, I imagine, for us to cover everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose it depends on what you want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I hope everything we say is relevant and directly to the point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: How long will you take with your witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I was just going to inform you of this and my apologies for not having done so earlier. We had indicated the times that we are going to use for the testimonies of each of the witness. However, I believe that we are actually going to spend less time, and we will be well within the boundary of two days. Only the witness who is testifying now will be testifying for a lengthier period of time, but that still will be within two hours. I believe that the other witnesses will take considerably less, and I believe that we will be done all the other witnesses by tomorrow at noon, which means that we also will complete the testimonies of all our witnesses within one single day. As to the issue of the closing remarks, if the Prosecution is announcing an hour per accused, then we would like it in writing so that we, ourselves, could get prepared, and obviously not as long this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: No, no. The writing of submissions on the closing speeches is not necessary. We asked counsel to make submissions in writing. All you need do is round up whatever submissions you want to make in review of the fact that you have led witnesses. It's not necessary. I'm sure his one hour is not in respect of each witness or in respect of each accused. That's very unlikely. It might be in respect of all of them. You can listen to what he will say within that period, and they are not unfamiliar things and things which you have already led. It is evidence which you have led which he is touching on. I don't think he needs to indicate any such thing in writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Maybe my words were not interpreted correctly. I did not say that we were going to make any written submissions. We just wanted to have an opportunity to address you orally afterwards, even if it is within a 10-minute or 15-minute scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought so. I thought that is a normal thing in proceedings of this nature. You merely make closing submissions which are just summaries of what has been said.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: If I might just ask one more question? As Ms. Residovic says that she's going to be finished by tomorrow noon, then I assume that we don't do these closing arguments on Friday, as we'd thought, but it will be right after lunch on Thursday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will continue on with that. Let's carry on with your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May I please have the witness Alija Buturovic recalled?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly remind the witness that he is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I do remind you, Witness, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, before the break, we discussed how Mr. Delalic, on several occasions, helped you accommodate the refugees. Mr. Buturovic, can you now tell me whether this was the only big problem that the town of Konjic and you had to face?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: This was only one of the problems which I had to deal with in the post which I had. As early as late April and early May, there were about 15.000 refugees in Konjic, and there were another 22.000 in transit, which went through the so-called salvation road to Dalmacija, so this was one of the problems. Another problem was the accommodation and reception of these refugees, which was very difficult due to the constant shelling of the town. The residential structures, apartment blocks, private houses, school buildings, and factories were all on fire and affected. It was a very complicated situation. With respect to the accommodation of refugees, a further problem posed was the fact that Konjic did not have a single hotel. It only had a small motel with about 40 beds, so that was the second problem. The third problem was a very severe lack of food stuffs and medicine. The entire population, regardless of their social status, within one month were left without any reserves in food, in money, or all other needs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In these severe shortages, you still took care of the civilian population. Can you tell me whether Zejnil Delalic, in this period of April through June and through the summer of 1992, also helped you with his private means, in other words, with his personal contributions, in order to resolve these problems? If he did so, can you please say how he did it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: As the president of this municipal body, I was in charge of the accommodation and providing food. I was pressured to constantly work in great haste in order to keep abreast with the situation. My colleagues and I, we all had to coordinate with the humanitarian organisations in town. I personally went to the Lenna Eloka (phoen) in Split to the president of Merhamet. Since Zejnil Delalic had a wide circle of associates and friends outside the former Yugoslavia, I asked him to help us get in touch with them. From his personal reserves, we, several times, received canned food, tea, medicine, and a colleague of mine did this. There were also individuals who reported there, regardless of what ethnic background they were from.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that the town was heavily shelled. What were the consequences of this and did you have any communications with Mr. Delalic in that regard? What was his position on this?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Because of this situation, which was very difficult, I sought advice from anyone that I thought could help us, either by advice or by some concrete measures. Zejnil Delalic would come up with a number of suggestions in passing, as it were, especially after the siege of Bradina was lifted. Following that event, we talked and I told him that we were facing a humanitarian catastrophy in Konjic, that we had no way out, and I recall his words, he said, "My comrade, Alija, we are all in a very difficult situation, but the Serbs in Donje Selo are in the worst situation." I am mentioning this because of this shelling in Konjic. Because of the severe shortages, an anti-Serb feeling or atmosphere was growing in Konjic. This was manifested in different ways in the municipality. However, I believe that my colleague, myself, and Mr. Delalic agreed on this, and we acted accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The words you have just quoted and which you remember which Mr. Delalic told you in a conversation, that everybody was in a difficult situation, but the Serbs in Donje Selo were in a worse situation, does that suggest to you and did he urge you to pay equal attention to all sides, to all people affected in the area?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: In the first months of the war, practically no humanitarian organisation reached Konjic. Most of these humanitarian convoys went to Sarajevo and Central Bosnia. At first, the supplies for the population were certain symbolic humanitarian organisations of Muslims called Merhamet, and Caritas, a Croatian, that is, Catholic organisation. This aid could not have been fully distributed to everybody who was in need. The War Presidency, at that time, instructed us to set up criteria for the distribution of aid, and my team worked on that. They would provide lists of people and needs, let's say, a quarter kilo of flour or a quart of oil, and it went to Merhamet, Caritas, and to the Red Cross. We had people who would come there, and we had to ask the police to keep order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ask him to give an answer to the question you have put. He has not answered that question but given a lengthy explanation to other matters which we are not interested in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is precisely what I was trying to suggest to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, please, my question to you was: In light of everything you just told us, did Zejnil Delalic, in this conversation, tell you what his position was, whether these Serbs in Donje Selo should be treated in the same way, using the same criteria, as everybody else?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He explicitly told me, and we had a brief consultation on this issue, and he said, not only the Serbs, but all other non-Muslim population was treated in the exact same way, by the same criteria, from the first day of the war until today. This is the policy that has been kept and maintained throughout.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, you said that you were president of the Municipal Staff for refugees. In this staff, did you have coordinators who coordinated with other humanitarian organisations in town?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because of the complicated situation, this staff was renamed into a coordinating board for relocation of refugees and the reception and distribution of humanitarian aid. This body received additional duties and tasks, and there were coordinators who were coordinating between us and the local humanitarian organisation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, before the war, the population in Konjic was mixed, and in 1992, this was the case also. What was the composition of your coordination board by ethnic background, and I mean in Konjic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I was the president of the coordinating board, and I believe that there were seven or eight additional members of the board. I know that Husein Dzambas represented Merhamet. Fra Drago Colak represented Caritas. The Konjic Hospital was represented by Dr. Marijan Mic. The Red Cross was represented by --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you just tell us what ethnic background these members were from? Were they all from one ethnic group or from different ones?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: The board was multi-ethnic. There were Muslims, Croats, and Serbs represented in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, a moment ago you said that the international organisations did not, for awhile, respond to this humanitarian catastrophy in Konjic. Can you tell us, when did the first convoy of an international organisation with supplies reach the town and what did they bring?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: The first convoy, which was an UNHCR convoy, entered Konjic on the 18th of August, 1992. Again, due to shelling, it took it six hours to get in and unload. It was a small convoy which brought about 60 tons worth of supplies, 30 tons out of which were flour, and the rest were beans, some salt, and there was tomato puree. This was a symbolic shipment which reached this town to just alleviate the situation and prevent the worst.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, is that when the first blankets also reached town?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I do not recall that they arrived with that shipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't follow where this is leading us. I can understand, perhaps, if Mr. Buturovic was to be sentenced, that this may have some relevance, but unless it is going to be brought together and we're going to be shown something at the end, at this stage, I fail to see what the relevance is of shipments of blankets and tomato puree arriving in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: And the connection of Mr. Delalic to these supplies. We're only concerned with Zejnil Delalic, not how the relief supplies reached Konjic. We're more interested in the role of Mr. Zejnil Delalic. We have evidence about the shortages there. We're not interested in all that. We want to know the role played by Mr. Zejnil Delalic in these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours. I am absolutely convinced what the witness is talking about. I am surprised that the Prosecution seems not to be, because we are talking about the circumstances in which these criminal offences actually occurred, that is, the circumstances and the living conditions in Konjic at the relevant time. If we look at the Tadic judgement, and it is, again, something that was brought up yesterday with Professor Tomic, I believe that it is pertinent to hear a witness who has facts about the situation and the role of Mr. Delalic in alleviating this situation. This was the purpose of these questions, in other words, the circumstances, the broader circumstances in which these criminal offences took place and which are all charged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I have two responses to that. One is the problem I'm having in seeing how it's related to Mr. Delalic. The second problem I have is, of course, if counsel sees that this is an important mitigating issue and wants to raise it, that's, by all means, up to her to do so, as long as Your Honours consider that to be the case. But, of course, it broadens the whole issue and makes my need to cross-examine much more wider than I would have otherwise done in relation to pure mitigation issues, because I'm afraid it's gone much wider than what would ordinarily be required simply to establish mitigation. As for the Tadic case, the general circumstances surrounding Kozarac and Prijedor at the time were matters that were raised during the course of the trial and not in mitigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, the issue of the general social conditions and issues have been matters which, all along in this trial, have been emphasised and referred to as relevant points and such evidence might have been given. But what is important in this sequence now is the role of Delalic relating to mitigation of possible guilt against him. So I don't really see how these general conditions are matters which could be relevant. These are general conditions. These are not matters related to his own activity, and I don't think you need to go that far. Because if we are picking on all the general social conditions in a place, there can be no limits to what we can refer to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I just want to remind you that the Prosecutor's witness Miro Golubovic spoke about the flour that was included in the convoy to Donje Selo, and I'm going to ask this witness about that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of August when that convoy arrived, did you, at that time, that is, the middle of August, discuss this issue with Zejnil Delalic, since you were influenced by certain opinions at the time that the Serbs should be treated in a different way?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Prior to the arrival of the convoy which took place on the 18th of August, I had several opportunities to meet Zejnil Delalic. There was the manifestation of oath taking in Celebici, and I was glad to hear that he was coming. On that occasion, he told me, "Alija, please, do not forget the Serbs from Donje Selo."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I had serious problems with my team. I had to convince them that a certain amount of food should also be distributed to the refugees in Donje Selo. From that first convoy, UNHCR convoy, we took certain amounts, a certain quantity of flour for them. The delivery note was signed by Mr. Zoran Cerkez, and he took the supplies to Donje Selo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to this particular conversation and everything that you have stated about Zejnil Delalic in this regard, Mr. Buturovic, what do you think? Throughout that period, throughout the war, did Zejnil Delalic continue to behave the same way? Did he remain the same kind of person? Did he retain the same type of attitude towards other people, and did he still sympathise with everyone?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: My personal opinion, and I feel very strong about it, is that Zejnil Delalic remained the same person as he was before the war. He sympathised with everybody else's suffering the same way, and this can be illustrated with several examples. He acted accordingly in several very specific occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To the extent that you know Mr. Zejnil Delalic, do you think that he was able to do any harm to any man?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I'm strongly convinced that he was unable to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Such a man who, in spite of the war conditions and adverse circumstances which led to strong anti-Serb feelings in the area, did that man, who you know very well, agree with any other type of activity, activity that was carried out by some third persons who wished to harm Serbs or any other people in the area?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I'm firmly convinced that he never tried to impose his opinion on anyone else, and I believe that he was sensitised to the problems at that time. He was a tolerant person and he could listen to others. When he told me about the situation in Donje Selo and the flour that was needed, he said, "Alija, I know you might have a lot of problems because of that," and, indeed, I did have them, and I was severely criticised both by the war presidency and the coordination board because I first sent supplies to Donje Selo, and only later on to refugee centres and the head centre in Konjic, which, at the time, was crowded with patients and wounded persons. I did that before I distributed aid to any other social institution in the area, and I believe that it was the right thing to do at the time, and I believe I did the right thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Court is already familiar with the fact that in the month of November, Mr. Delalic left the town of Konjic. You probably know that he was a victim of very intense propaganda, but this is not something I'm going to ask you about. I would like to know whether you have any knowledge of Mr. Zejnil Delalic continuing to help the population of Konjic in general, regardless of their ethnic or religious background. If you know of any such activity, could you explain to us how is it that you know?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I know several examples of Mr. Delalic helping other people. Certain individuals were able to leave the area, certain were not. He helped with providing accommodation of all victims of the war, people who were severely wounded or sick people. At the beginning when Konjic was under a complete blockade, when it was not possible to receive any food or any supplies, the local commune organised an alternative way of bringing supplies into the town, by parachuting. My colleague was a member of the committee that was in charge of that, and I was once told that the supplies that were, in this way, brought to town, very often brought the titled inscription, "The assistance provided by Mr. Zejnil Delalic."

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After all that you have said about Mr. Zejnil Delalic, if you had to describe his personality in a few words, what would you say? What kind of person is Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: In short, I would say that he's a highly moral, ethical person, that he's humane, that he's cosmopolitan. Once again, let me state that I could never accept that he's the man who ever distinguished, on the grounds of ethnicity, nationality, or anything else, when it comes to the population of our town, the town of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, in view of your knowledge of the situation in Konjic at that time and later on, I wish to ask you a few more questions. You are still acting as the head of the institution for social work. Are you involved in any activities relating to the return of refugees to the town of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: The public institution that is involved with social work in Konjic deals with problems such as child protection, juvenile delinquency, family treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer my question precisely?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Ever since the beginning when it was created --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, how could this be, in any way, relevant, to mitigation, I fail to see, Your Honours. I mean, this has nothing to do with mitigation of Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really fail to understand my learned colleague. He claims in his written submission that refugees cannot return to Konjic. I fail to see what that has to do with the mitigation of anyone, and this is what Mr. Niemann wrote in his written submission. Here is the man who is in a position to tell us whether anyone is coming back to Konjic, whether the Serbs are coming back to Konjic and what is happening to them. Are these not mitigating circumstances for everyone, including my client?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: What is the relevance of the question of what is being said as to what evidence you want to lead? It's not that he hasn't written certain things. He might have written them, but what is that relevance to what you intend to lead your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The fact that Konjic is an open town where Serbs are returning, and they are returning to Zejnil Delalic's house, and it has definitely something to do with Zejnil Delalic, but it also goes to the general conditions in this area. People are coming back, including those who spent some time in the prison in Celebici. I'm also referring to Petko Gruvac. His family has also submitted an application to come back to Konjic. I would like that this witness be given an opportunity to provide you with the truthful information. We're trying, endeavouring, to provide this Court with relevant and accurate information which is important for the consequences of the alleged criminal offences. This is something that is very important when it comes to determining the appropriate sentence and can be considered as mitigating circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Provided, Your Honours, that we can rebut this by producing evidence from the SFOR, from the International Community, from the current policy of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who are all actively involved in encouraging people to come back to different parts of the country which have been unsettled, and provided, of course, that it can be shown that the people returning to the Konjic area at the moment are doing so directly as a result of something that Mr. Delalic did. If that's established, then, of course, I will, gladly, withdraw my objection. There's just an assumption here, this huge leap of an assumption, that all these people are coming back now because Mr. Delalic's did something for their benefit. I submit, Your Honour, that there are a whole lot of things out there that have caused them to come back and they have precious little to do with Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I know what is coming, the evidence that she wants to present is. Mr. Niemann presented to the Trial Chamber, in aggravation of punishment, a written statement by Dr. Petko Gruvac that makes certain factual allegations that Mr. Niemann has presented to this Trial Chamber as statements of the truth, in aggravation of punishment. I believe that Mrs. Residovic may have in her possession, documentation to show, to at least cast doubt on the credibility of the factual statements that were presented to the Trial Chamber by the Prosecutor in aggravation. I think that that's highly relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, the view I hold, and I suppose my colleagues also do, is there is very little that should be excluded in aggravation or in mitigation, except if it is inadmissible. If evidence could be admitted to show either way, I think it should be admitted. It depends, of course, in examining, that you find that it is irrelevant for the purposes which it was introduced. I think you could lead the evidence and leave us to determine whether it is material for the purposes of mitigation or aggravation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and I will kindly ask you to let me continue, because I'm to deal with an issue, an allegation having to do with ethnic cleansing that is contained in the submission of the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, would you please try to answer my questions briefly and precisely. I have just a few more questions for you. Tell us, Mr. Buturovic, do you have a database available at your institute regarding the movement of the refugees in Konjic, refugees and displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How many refugees from other areas of the Republic still reside in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: There is over 8.000 displaced persons still living in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You stayed in Konjic throughout the war. You are in a position to tell us, Mr. Buturovic, whether anyone expelled by force from residential areas, your friends, Serbs, and if they left the town, do you know in what manner they did so?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: We have to go back to the year 1992 and the month of April. The majority of Serbs, upon the invitation, upon an appeal of the Serb Democratic Party, left the town of Konjic and went to a nearby area where they established a so-called Serbian municipality of Konjic. A large number of Croats and Muslims also left the town at the time because of the war, because they were fearful for their lives. So one cannot speak about expulsions by force.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, were there any Serbs who stayed in the town of Konjic and who endured the same difficult situation that you did?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were quite a few of them who stayed throughout the war, and they shared, with us, the burden of the war, the good things and the bad things. These people are still residing in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to 1992 and maybe even later. Were there any Serbs who held key positions in the town of Konjic at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I can recall a certain number of Serbs, including the example of a very good friend of mine, Mr. Dragan Andric, who held a very high rank in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. He has stayed in Konjic, and he's a very successful businessman today. I can give you another example, that of Mr. Nedeljko Stojanovic, who was the director of the electrical company in town, and he is still employed with the same company. He is a very respectable citizen. He is a member of the group that was established by the municipal counsel, and they are in charge of humanitarian projects in the town. They are coordinating various humanitarian projects in Konjic. Further on, in my own institution, there is Mr. Milutin Milosevic, a professor of sociology, who has spent the entire war in Konjic. Mr. Mirko Mirovic is the director of the largest elementary school in Konjic which has 2.000 students. He is still living in Konjic, and he was in Konjic throughout the war. I can think of countless other examples.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you can, Mr. Buturovic, but I believe that this is enough for the Court. Since you probably know, as a citizen of Konjic, that some Serbs were detained in the prison in Celebici, could you tell us, do you know whether any of these detainees, after they were released from Celebici, did they stay and live with you in Konjic throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: One part of them, that is, some of the inmates in Celebici, left, and I know of a number of them who have stayed in Konjic. I know, for example, Mirko Mrkajic who is working for a very respectable organisation that is in charge of the return of refugees to Konjic. I know, for example, Zarko Kulas who runs a very successful shop in Konjic. It's an Adidas shop and he has a large number of employees. I also know Mirko Kuljanin from the town of Brdjani, who is a farmer, and he used to be a farmer before the war. He has a lot of sheep and pigs. He has a large farm.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Buturovic. I think this will be enough. You don't have to remember every single one of them. Mr. Buturovic, the people who left Konjic through various ways, as refugees, through exchanges and so on, whether these people were of Serbian nationality, do you know whether they are coming back to Konjic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: There has been a very intensive process of return in Konjic that's been going on for quite awhile, not only Serbs, but it also involves Croats and Muslims who, for various reasons, left the town. This information can be found in our database at the institution where I work. I know, for example, that over 300 Serb families, that is, some 900 persons, have registered with the municipality board, for return, which is involved in providing accommodation and returning property and so on. I know of 22 or 50 cases, 50 families that have come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you linking this evidence with any contribution by Delalic in any of his activities, the evidence now being led?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The mitigating circumstances in their entirety are balanced with the totality of aggravating circumstances that have been offered by the Prosecution. My next question relates to other allegations of the Prosecution, namely, that the property of these people has been confiscated and similar allegations. These allegations have been mentioned in the case of the Prosecutor, and they have been labelled as aggravating circumstances, but I'm afraid they are not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the whole point is being missed here. There is a disjunction between people leaving the town because of the circumstances which we allege were created by these accused, and them coming back now. I mean, if it could be shown that the people coming back now are doing so because of something which Mr. Delalic or the other accused did, then, perhaps, there may be some relevance, but we all know that there are a whole host of other reasons, primarily the intervention of the International Community, which is causing these people to come back. For these people coming back, to be attributed in this way to Mr. Delalic, without any evidence at all that that's the case, Your Honours, must be objectionable.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, was the town of Konjic the first town to receive the title of an open city because of its multi-ethnic character to which Mr. Zejnil Delalic made his contribution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't think this is mitigating factors to your client, then you may not lead any evidence towards that. If you talk about a general situation, which is the normal restoration of peace, when something has happened takes place, and this is what is happening here. It's not because any of the accused persons contributed to what is happening. Mitigating factors are matters which have been contributed by these persons themselves. I don't see what you're trying to show, because that was why I asked you whether the evidence which Mr. Buturovic was giving has any relationship with the contribution of Delalic, but you are still talking about general conditions which are happening because of the International Community's attitude towards restoration of peace and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, do you know that in 1992, when you met with Mr. Zejnil Delalic occasionally, do you know whether he continued seeing all his friends, regardless of their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You stated that your friend, Dragan Andric, you mentioned Dragan Andric, was he also a friend of Mr. Zejnil Delalic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the brief encounters in his house in 1992, could you come across members of all ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what ethnic background was the secretary, that is, the house mistress of his house in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: It was Mrs. Mira Pusalic, and she's a Croat by nationality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, in 1992, Zejnil Delalic worked towards the multi-ethnic aspect of the town of Konjic? Was his example followed?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have to say that Konjic was observed by the members of the International Community throughout the war, and the distribution of humanitarian aid was closely monitored. When the International Community proclaimed Konjic as an open city, it, indeed, took place. It took place on the 1st of July, 1997, and Mr. Zejnil Delalic definitely contributed to Konjic being proclaimed the first open city in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, do you know what ethnic background Mr. Delalic's wife is. It's Gordana and she is from Belgrade, and I presume that she's a Serb. Did she come to Konjic? Did she come to Konjic recently and did she stay at the family house?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I've seen her for the past several months on several occasions, and I had an opportunity to talk to her.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, do you know whether now, as earlier in 1992 and before the war, do you know that members of all nationalities are still coming to the family house of Zejnil Delalic as very good friends and well-intentioned people?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Petko and Gordana Grubac?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I know Mr. Petko Grubac. He is a very respectable neuropsychiatrist who lived in the same neighbourhood and I also know his wife, Gordana, and I know her very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to meet with any of them this year?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Gordana Grubac came to see me, to my office. She came to apply to return. It is an administrative procedure. It involves applying for the restitution of property. She had no problems in doing that, and she asked the tenant who is currently living in her apartment whether she can come to the apartment and take a few of her personal belongings, and I know that she did go there and there was no problem in contacting that person.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is, perhaps, not all necessary, but did she express her wish to come back and live in Konjic when you met her?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, she did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, since your institution has this relevant database, have you received the request of the Defence of Zejnil Delalic to be provided with the relevant data, and did you give that database to the president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the end, Mr. Buturovic, there is one more question that I would like to ask you. You knew Mr. Zejnil Delalic as a young man and as an adult. Was he an emotional person? Was he just is his behaviour and attitude towards other people?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: He was a very fine person, emotional person. He was a just person. He was ready to help, and he was, as I already told you, cosmopolitan and humane, and I think very highly of him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you trust him?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, I do not intend to hurt you in any way, but you are one of the people who have suffered severely in this war. The Court had an opportunity to see on the videotape that your apartment was one of the first apartments to be destroyed in this war, and you had a personal tragedy. Your child is an invalid as a result of the war. But can you tell me what you gave me as an answer when I previously asked you about Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: What I said was more or less the following: I said that if Zejnil Delalic were still here before the war, I would not have any problems. I know that I now have to take my son to Tel Aviv for a very complicated surgery which will cost me 40.000 German marks, but if Zejnil Delalic were here before the war, I wouldn't have any problems to find that money.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, when you came to The Hague, you provided me with some original documents relating to the receipt of the humanitarian aid, and the flour, in particular. You provided me with some information relating to the coordination board and also with a list of people who received that flour in Donje Selo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have given these documents to the Prosecutor, and if you have no objections, I would like to tender them. These are documents relating to the situation in 1991. I believe they go to the mitigation, but if you don't deem them relevant, we do not insist. However, these are the original documents that were supplied by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Anything you find necessary to show, you may tender them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then I will ask the usher's assistance -- okay. I can do it later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In view of Your Honours' ruling, I don't suppose there is much that I can do but, I do object to the relevance because there is no connection with Zejnil Delalic at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They have nothing to do with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, not on their face.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have additional copies for the Trial Chamber, and I have already provided a copy to the Prosecution, and they will be in support of the testimony of this witness. These are not original documents. Obviously, they are all photocopies. This concludes my examination of my witness, and I would like to thank him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You have no objection to the relevance of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'll explore it in cross-examination, Your Honours. Maybe I can find some relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination of this witness? Any examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLER
utterances.text: We have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution have any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, you said that Mr. Delalic made a contribution to the town of Konjic being declared an open town in 1997. Can you tell us the details of the contribution he made towards that end?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: The International Community considered for awhile whether Konjic would be given the status of an open city, and it monitored the situation in Konjic from the beginning of the aggression. The representatives of the international organisations knew that from the beginning of the war, all people in Konjic, regardless of what their names were, regardless of which of the three groups they belonged to, were treated in a just and equal way. It was well-known that the humanitarian aid was evenly distributed. I followed, very closely, this whole period, and everything that went on in 1992 ultimately resulted or contributed to Konjic being given the status of an open city.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What specifically did the International Community acknowledge in relation to Mr. Delalic himself concerning this issue of whether or not Konjic would become an open town in 1997?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: His attitude towards the local population, regardless of who they were, he is a person who advocated that people not be distinguished by their background, but that they would all be treated in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where might we find this acknowledgement by the International Community? Is there some documentation or publication which is being produced which expressly mentions the name of Mr. Zejnil Delalic and his contribution to this end?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object to this question. The witness said that it was a general contribution to creating conditions and prevailing attitudes in this town.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: No single individual received such acknowledgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My friend misquotes the transcript. If she cares to look at it, she will see that the witness said in his evidence that Mr. Delalic made a contribution to this, and that is merely what I was exploring. I think we now have the answer from the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When Mr. Delalic spoke to you about providing aid to the Serbs in Donje Selo, from what position of authority, if any, was he speaking to you?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, this question is a question of responsibility. It does not fall in the ambit of mitigating circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Counsel led this evidence, Your Honour, amidst some of my objections, and she leads this material on such a broad base. It is appropriate, in my submission, and entirely relevant to explore whether what he did was something as a consequence of his own emotion or as a consequence of the position he held. She calls it mitigating evidence, and she has done the same thing in her written submissions on a vast number of matters in a similar vein, then it is done and we have to respond to it. I am merely exploring that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is a perfectly legitimate question. I think the witness might be able to explain the circumstance and the scope of what was done. I don't think there is any ambiguity in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The witness will say so, but I would not like to have my questions misquoted. They are there in the transcript because the witness has spoken about his personal meetings and conversations with my client.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If there's any inference, Your Honour, that I'm misquoting the transcript, then I refute that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, sir, I asked you a moment ago what position of authority, if any, did Mr. Delalic rely upon in order to advise you that the people of Donje Selo should be given aid, along with other persons in the Konjic municipality, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: That occasion was an oath-taking ceremony for the members of the BH army. This is when we met, and I don't think he said it should, he said, "Alija, we are all in a difficult situation, and perhaps the Serbs in Donje Selo are in the worst situation." He didn't say whether things should be done or must be done. It was just sort of a hint. It was a suggestion, and I took it as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That satisfies your question. He didn't say anything in any capacity whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was an occasion when he was dressed in military uniform, was it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This occasion was at the Celebici barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry. Could the witness please repeat his answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He said it was an oath-taking occasion when it was done at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did this occasion, when he spoke to you, was this at the Celebici barracks when the oath-taking ceremony took place and when he was dressed in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I personally was in front of the barracks. I did not enter the barracks. I was not a military person. I did not have a specific task to go there. I just came for this ceremony of oath-taking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On that occasion, did he suggest to you that the Serbs that were either in Celebici or the families of Serbs that were in Celebici should receive special aid and assistance as well?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: No. He just expressed his opinion to me. He said that I should never succumb to the anti-Serbian sentiment which prevailed in the town of Konjic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the Serbs that were in Donje Selo where Mr. Delalic had suggested should be given aid, they were refugees from Bradina, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: A number of Serbs from Donje Selo remained in Donje Selo, and a number of them were given the status of refugees from Bradina, which was sort of a privileged refugee position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These refugees, I take it, from Bradina, were there because of the war?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Unlike other suburban or outlying municipal areas was by and large spared, so very few shells ever landed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You spoke of the fact that there were quite a few Serbs who stayed in Konjic during the period of the war and continue to stay there. Would that be a figure of less than, say, two per cent or two per cent of the Serbs who were originally there?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I do not have the statistical data before me right now. I think that it's more than two per cent. I don't know. It may be closer to five, but I really don't have the right information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If I was to say to you that during the course of these proceedings there's been evidence presented before the Tribunal, in the form of a report by the UNHCR, saying that only about two per cent of the Serbs who originally were in Konjic remained in Konjic. You wouldn't have any figures to disagree with that, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question, if it was in the form of a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. It was in the form of a question. What I'm saying to you is if there's been evidence given before this Tribunal that, in 1994, the UNHCR reported that not more than two per cent of the Serbs who originally were in Konjic remained in Konjic at that time, you don't have any figures that would disagree with that, I take it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I do not have any figures, but I believe that it is at least five per cent of the Serbs. In fact, in my database in my computer, the representatives of the UNHCR actually did visit our office and used that information from the database we had, but I'm sure that the figure is higher. This is not just Konjic, it's Celebici, Podarasac, and Donje Selo. This is what I had in mind when I spoke about Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You spoke of refugees going to buildings and so forth in Donje Selo and around Konjic city itself. Why weren't refugees placed in Celebici, in the Celebici barracks? Do you know? Do you know the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I do not know the reason for it. I don't know what the barracks functioned as. I was in civilian structures. I did my job honestly, and I do not know what happened with the military facilities then. I do not know what is going on there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You testified about a visit by Mrs. Grubac when she came to you and sought authorisation to go to her previous premises and collect her property. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why did she need authorisation to go to her own house to collect her own property?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: She didn't need my permission. She came to me as the first door neighbour because we lived door to door and to a former good friend and, in fact, we have remained good friends. I did not give her permission. I just directed her to a window where she had to go and submit an application. It was with this official which we went, and this permission came from him. She took a number of her possessions which she wanted. She did not need my permission to do so at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm very sorry if I attributed that to you incorrectly. Perhaps you might be able to help me with this, though. Why would it be necessary for her to go to any official in the Konjic municipality in order to visit her own house in order to collect her own furniture? Can you help me with that?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I think this has a very simple explanation. Any person desiring to return to a place where they own a residence, they first have to report to the municipal authority to see whether somebody has moved into this apartment on a temporary basis, whether this apartment is still standing, whether it is in a condition fit for living. This lady came to an office which has been established by the municipality at the instigation of an American agency. She came to this office, and she said, "I have an apartment in Marshal Tito Street 36, and I want to be able to go back there." Then she first received information about the condition of her apartment there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know why she took her furniture and affects away if she intended to return?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: She took what she requested. She may not have found everything. Maybe some things were removed. Maybe some things were destroyed, but she submitted a form to the municipal authorities, and she requested to return to the apartment which she legally owns. She wants to go back to it when all the conditions for this are met.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I just briefly wish to turn to the exhibits that have been tendered through you in relation to your evidence, and I don't have the numbers of them, but might those exhibits be given to the witness? I understand it's 196/1, 197/1, and 198/1.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. They are not yet finished. I am going to forward the remaining of them. I'm just finishing numbering the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What is in these documents you want to examine?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I wish to find out why they are relevant to mitigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could these exhibits be given -- might I ask of the registrar, have I got the originals? Might the exhibits be given to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There are a number of names mentioned which are normally Serb names, Cerkez --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't possess detailed knowledge of these things. I've found on numerous occasions, Your Honours, that they are not always consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you just look at Exhibit 196/1 for me, please? This is a decision of the War Presidency of Konjic.
