Just in order that we may speed up this process, I'm really only interested in determining why they relate specifically to Mr. Delalic and why they would be tendered in assistance of any mitigation plea that he might have. Just dealing with that first one, was Mr. Delalic, in some way, connected, was he, to the War Presidency that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zejnil Delalic was, in a way, just as all the other members here, he was a coordinator between the army and the municipal authorities in tasks which were set by the War Presidency. Every member of this body, Fra Drago Colak coordinator for Caritas, Mr. Dzambas for Merhamet, and then there was Nadira Buturovic for health protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. We don't need to go through all of them, but perhaps you might help me then. Are you saying that in his position as coordinator, on military matters, that he was able to sort of coordinate your activities as well? Is that what you're saying? I'm just trying to explore this, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In relation to military matters --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Objection again, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He did not mention military matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'll withdraw that then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As a coordinator, you said between the army and the municipal authorities, and I should use exactly those words. In Mr. Delalic's capacity as coordinator between the army and the municipal authorities, was he able to in some way contribute to your activities in relation to your board, was he?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Objection, again, because the Prosecutor is moving into the area of responsibility of Mr. Delalic, whereas the witness was just trying to point out the ethnic composition of this board, which included Serbs, Muslims and Croats in 1992. I don't think that any of my questions to this witness went in the direction of establishing anything about my client's responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose what the witness was doing was to indicate how effective, perhaps, Delalic was towards him, although, as he said, it was in his ordinary, private capacity. He did not suggest that he had any other capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's her documents. I'm merely exploring them. She put them in, and I'm just merely trying to find out what they mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: She said that this document was used to show that the coordination board was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I heard her say that, Your Honour, but I'm as a total loss to understand why that has anything to do with the mitigation of any sentence to be imposed on Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: She was trying to answer your argument that the Serbs were thrown out of Konjic because of the conduct of these persons, because he was talking about the severity of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I thought she was talking about their return, and I thought that was to do with an entirely different situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What she's saying is this document shows that the Serbs are still there and they were taking part in these activities, for example, this coordination board. It also had Serb members.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we will have to stop now and come back at 4.30 to allow you to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, I was showing you a document, Exhibit 196. Is it your evidence that some of the names listed there, being the composition of the board, that some of those persons were Serbs, were they?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Vesna Bektasevic, for example, she's a journalist of the Konjic radio station, and she has retained her function. She had the duty to inform people about the decisions reached by our board.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this the committee or board that was opposed to you providing aid to Donje Selo?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So this board was in favour of that, was it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell me why it is that you believe that Mr. Delalic himself is, in some way, connected with this document in terms of mitigation of his sentence? Do you know the reason for that, in what way he is connected to it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I have indicated, on several occasions, that I had personal and friendly connections with Mr. Delalic, and I would consult him very often on various matters. This was something that was not binding in any way. We had our common opinions. We thought that we should reach Donje Selo with our supplies first. I have a delivery note here from which you can clearly see that it was the village of Donje Selo that received the aid in the first place. This was followed by the health centre in Konjic and the bakery which supplied bread for refugee centres, and then came local communes and the other people who were in need of help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But apart from Mr. Delalic being a person who suggested that you might give it to people in Donje Selo, he has no other connection whatsoever to these documents, does he?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I thought you said in your evidence, and I may be wrong on this, that some personal board or committee in authority was against you giving food to the Serbs in Donje Selo. Can you tell me who it was that was against this giving of food to the Serbs in Donje Selo?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: The coordination board was in charge of coordinating activities between Merhamet, Caritas, the Red Cross organisation, and the centre for social work. It was appointed and established by the War Presidency of the municipality, which was the first executive body of the municipality in that period. Prior to the delivery, prior to the distribution of humanitarian aid, we had to inform, thereafter, the War Presidency. I was asked by the person in charge, by the person who was sitting on the War Presidency, why the aid should go to Donje Selo first. There was a lot of criticism, for example, from the president of the economic body, which was also appointed by the War Presidency. This economic body, economic council, consisted of some very respectable businessmen in the area. It was these people who criticised me and who didn't like the idea of the first delivery to be carried out in Donje Selo. The War Presidency and the health centre, they were the only civilian institutions that were working in the town during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This flour, wasn't this provided by the UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the UNHCR that provided it to the coordination board.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, if the UNHCR was providing flour, it certainly would insist that it not be restricted to one ethnic group, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He has answered the question. He said that there was a lot of anti-Serb feelings in the town from the local people. There was an anti-Serb feeling in the town because of the shelling and so on, and maybe people felt very strongly that "We should feed ourselves first before giving it to the Serb population."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: My suggestion, Your Honour, is that the UNHCR, who gives the aid, would determine who it goes to, and certainly any suggestion of it going to just Muslims and just Serbs and not Croats would be totally unacceptable to the UNHCR, and that's the point I make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I didn't think that is what he wants. I think he meant that Donje Selo was the first call of problem. Why should he go there first? That is the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand two aspects of the evidence, Your Honour. One is why it goes first and why at all, and he tells us that it was because Mr. Delalic had said to him, "You must look after the people in Donje Selo." The point I'm trying to establish is whether -- it may be the people who gave the aid, namely, the UNHCR, who insisted that it be distributed, notwithstanding the ethnic division in the community, which is something we would expect the UNHCR to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I understand that in view of that anti-Serb feeling, it's the actual distributors who were more important in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think the UNHCR would be very quick to withdraw humanitarian aid or withdraw it from the distributors if it was discovered that it was being applied for one ethnic group only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That comes later, after the distribution has been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have a document here that was given to me by the Defence which they did not seek to tender which indicates, it seems to me, that the flour was provided by the UNHCR based in Split and not some local Red Cross or not some other charitable institution. I'll ask the witness to, perhaps, have a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Of course the coordination board didn't take into account that anti-Serb feeling when distributing the flour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The UNHCR certainly would have, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They would have objected, but if the coordination board would have given way to the anti-Serb feeling --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think that the problem may be, Your Honours, that if it was distributed only to the Muslim population of Konjic, and the Serbs who were held in Donje Selo were not to receive aid at the time, that that would be the last amount of aid that was going to be supplied to that community. So there may be another rational as to why it was distributed to the Serbs in Donje Selo, other than the humanitarian works and good nature of the accused, Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, please, if I may respond, and so that the record is clear, I wish to say that the witness did not state that Zejnil Delalic had told him that he should give the flour in Donje Selo, as quoted by Mr. Niemann. The witness told himself that it was the first delivery of flour that the International Community, that is, the UNHCR, sent to Konjic. There are no secret documents. Every document that has been discussed by this witness was given to the Prosecutor. We haven't given this to the Court, but we can do so right now so that the Court can see how the distribution went, but I don't think it's necessary, because the witness has answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, I think it might be necessary to complete the record, seeing where it comes from, because I think, from a reading of the transcript, there is some confusion as to its source. It certainly hasn't been made clear, until now, that it's come from the UNHCR. If I may, Your Honours, I think I would like to show this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's not really important. You can proceed further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It doesn't make any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, I objected to all the others, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't think it matters.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document D202/1 regarding the coordination board and accommodation of displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, this document, Exhibit 202, indicates, does it not, that the flour, 4.950 kilograms, was taken over from the UNHCR which, at that time, was based in Split, and it says specifically "For the refugees residing in Donje Selo"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Refugees. The Serbs were locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It says, "For the refugees in Donje Selo," Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Donje Selo was a Serb village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Donje Selo had refugees, and this witness has testified to that. This document says that it was taken over from the UNHCR for the refugees residing in Donje Selo. It's been submitted, Your Honours, through this witness and attempted to be established by documentation that the decision to give the humanitarian aid that was received to the Serbs was a consequence of something that Mr. Delalic said. Now, this document seems to suggest something entirely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What I've said you've not followed. The Serbs were the locals of Donje Selo, and this document talks about refugees. The refugees were the Muslims who would come from different parts of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's not my understanding of the evidence. My understanding of the evidence is that the refugees in Donje Selo came from Bradina. I asked the witness questions about that, and they were the Serbs from Donje Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is it not right that this document relates to flour received from the UNHCR based in Split specifically for refugees residing in Donje Selo?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: This document is a part of the form that we used at the so-called distribution centre, and the indicated quantity of goods was supposed to be distributed to the indicated area. Later, this would receive another form. It is understandable that this humanitarian aid, as well as every other humanitarian aid, went from Split to Sarajevo. That was the only way it could reach the relevant area. The shipment was intended for displaced persons and refugees. I believe that this document is quite clear. This was at the beginning of the war when we found ourselves in a completely different situation than before. The intention was an honourable one. UNHCR never said specifically that it should go to Donje Selo. It only indicated that the aid should reach the refugees and the displaced persons. The UNHCR trusted our committee, our board, in that they knew that we would be honest about distributing the food.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The refugees that were located in Donje Selo for the benefit of His Honour, in relation to His Honour's question, the refugees that were located in Donje Selo were, among others, Serbs that had been refugees from the military activity and fighting that occurred in Bradina; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the whole point of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, just one more question, Exhibit 197, if you could just have a look at that for me, please? Do I take it that this document implies that the flour was made into bread and it was then distributed in Donje Selo. Is that what it means?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: No. This document indicates that only eight days after the distribution of the flour to Donje Selo, the city bakery, which made bread for refugees and displaced persons only, that they brought 4.000 kilos of flour to the village only eight years after that. It was only after that period of time that the city bakery received flour to make bread for various places where cooked food was distributed in the town. Because of the situation and the circumstances, most of the population was in need of this type of distribution of food. It was the coordination board who organised that, and we collected food from various households in the town of Konjic. This is how we dealt with it on a daily basis. Donje Selo had the priority in receiving this food, and this was also approved by the UNHCR. They approved it also in respect of the Konjic Hospital where there were many wounded people. This is all part of the humanitarian work that we did at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The fact of the matter is that you had little say in it, though, isn't it, that the flour was provided by the UNHCR and was to be used to supply refugees, and you were given the task to distribute it to refugees; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It wouldn't have mattered one bit whether Mr. Delalic said, "Give it to the refugees or not." It had to go that way because it had been predetermined.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: No. Delalic merely expressed his opinion, and he never acted as anyone who had any kind of superior authority. He provided his opinion, and he said what I already quoted. He did not have any specific role in the distribution of the food.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It just so happened that his opinion coincided with the requirements dictated by the UNHCR; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: The UNHCR did not say that the flour should go there first. They simply trusted our board in matters of distribution. After the first donations, Konjic was the first town in Bosnia and Herzegovina in terms of quantity of food that was distributed, because and thanks to the work of the coordination board. We had enough food so we distributed food. We gave food away to Jablanica and other places so that people could survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I just wanted to tidy one thing up before I finished, in case I confused you, because I think I may have misquoted the evidence as it was. I spoke of the UNHCR figures relating to the percentage of Serbs in Konjic in 1994, their study in 1994. I think that I said that there was only two per cent left. Just to clarify it, and you can respond to it if you wish, but I just wish to clarify that what I intended to say was, it was two per cent of the population were Serbs in 1994 by this study, as opposed to 15 per cent prior to the war. If I confused you in any way and you wish to add to that, please do so now.

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: I believe that this is correct, that there were 50 (sic) per cent of the Serbs living there. What I said, the remainder of the Serbian population in 1992, I believe again that I can say it was about five per cent. The first census of the refugees and displaced persons and people who had stayed in their homes, the first census was taken in '93, but we're not talking only about the town of Konjic, because the town of Konjic has only a third of the total population of the entire Konjic municipality. I know the approximate data for the municipality overall, but not specifically only for the town of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I should say there are two things. We are speaking on the same terms. We're talking about the municipality. The other thing I noticed is the transcript said "50 per cent" of Serbs living there, and I said 15. Perhaps the transcript -- it's 15, not 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, my learned colleague of the Prosecution showed you a document, the document regarding the order to the distribution centre, suggesting that this flour was sent by the UNHCR for Donje Selo. Please tell us, was this quantity of flour part of the 30-town shipment which you mentioned previously?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This amount was distributed according to the criteria set up by your board?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The input of Mr. Delalic through personal conversation was just for you to reaffirm your own conviction that people should be treated in an equitable manner?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My next question relates to a question put by my learned colleague Niemann about a visit to Ms. Gruvac and going back to her apartment. When we talk about the --

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat this question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: People have a right to a residence, which could mean two things, either that it is their own ownership or property or that they live in a state-owned apartment?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: The tenant's right does not imply that they possess the apartment, but it gives them the right to return to this apartment when all the conditions for it are met.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that the private property of the Gruvac family, like their weekend house, continues to be their private property?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That continues to be their private property, unlike the apartment which is still socially owned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Further in regard to the Prosecutor's question, could you please tell me whether all apartments are socially or state-owned which were abandoned by their owners during the war, regardless of whether the people who have abandoned them were Serbs, Croats, or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is correct that the apartments which were abandoned during wartime, they were declared temporarily open or free. Then there was a body, a municipal body, which was put in charge of them. There was even a law that was passed regulating this issue. Again, let me try to emphasise, after the war, this law has been repealed. In Konjic, in the spirit of openness, it is the leading town in encouraging people to go back to their own residences. There were various reasons for people leaving Konjic. Some of them may have been fleeing conscription, different reasons, but they all still have -- they all still need to meet the same criteria and same standards. They all have to apply to the municipal authorities and go through due process.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Buturovic, perhaps you can say on the basis of your own example. Your own apartment was completely destroyed. Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: On 4th May, my apartment was shelled, and then subsequently a couple of more shells fell there. From the municipal authority, I was given the temporary residence of a friend, of a good friend. It was a smaller apartment, and I still live there. I personally applied for that colleague's residence to be returned to him, whereas, my own apartment is under reconstruction, and I hope to be able to go back there soon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And your colleague will go back to his own apartment?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He will go back to his own apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just as the Gruvac family are going to go back?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, just as the Gruvac family are going to go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The last question in response to the cross-examination by my learned colleague, with regard to the percentage of the Serbian population which has remained, and we are not going to try to determine it today, it probably exists in your data base, but since you mentioned it, is it true that the largest number of Serbian residents who left in 1992, left in April on a voluntary basis on instructions or call by the SDS?

utterances.speaker: ALIJA BUTUROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any other witnesses? We will discharge the present witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Buturovic. You are discharged.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D202/1 should be renumbered document 266.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I call as a witness Nebojsa Manigodjic.

utterances.speaker: THE USHER
utterances.text: Would you read out the oath, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may take your seat, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you please introduce yourself by stating your full name?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: My name is Nebojsa Manigodjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is your ethnic background and what is your citizenship?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: I'm a Serb and a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is your profession, sir?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: I'm an architect.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Zejnil Delalic, and if you do so, please tell the Court how long you've known him.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do know Zejnil Delalic. My acquaintance with him goes back to 1973, which is when he became a good acquaintance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Zejnil Delalic built a family home in Konjic and were you, in any way, involved in it?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do know this, and this is how my acquaintance with him started, because, as I told you, I'm an architect by profession. So we became better acquainted from that time when he was building his house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Zejnil Delalic used to live until then?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: Zejnil Delalic, that is, the Delalic family, had a family home in Ostrozac, and Zejnil Delalic lived in Germany at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When Zejnil Delalic's house was finished, did you continue to meet with Zejnil Delalic and did you meet in this house?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Our friendship after that continued, and we would meet whenever we managed. As I said, he lived in Germany, and this social circle, the old friends, somehow managed to get together and spend as much time as was possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Manigodjic, can you please tell the Court what kind of circle this was? What were these people by profession, by ethnic background, the circle of friends of Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: This was our, sort of, small group from Jablanica, as a core, and then there were a number of people from outside of that circle. There were some prominent persons there, both from the political arena and from entertainment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During this association with you, did Zejnil ever exhibit any intolerance or hostility towards people of other ethnic backgrounds in Konjic who were part of your group?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: No. I absolutely never noticed that by any detail, that he distinguished among any of these different groups, members of different groups, and that he treated them in any different way than us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So far as you know, Mr. Manigodjic, did Mr. Zejnil Delalic like people and help people and even some clubs and associations in Jablanica and Konjic? If you know so, please tell the Court about it.

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do know about this. I know quite well about it, and I can mention two examples of that where I also participated. This concerned an exchange which was established between two schools, one is in Jablanica and another one is a very small town near Frankfurt, Germany called Rodermark. These two schools are similar by their programmes or their curriculum, in fact. They specialised in instruction, and thanks to Mr. Delalic's acquaintance with teachers in that school, who also happened to be architects, we were able to come up with a project which brought these two schools together, and it was manifested through a visit, first, of the students of the German school, and these students came to Jablanica, and then the students from Jablanica returned to visit to this school in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Having known Zejnil Delalic, Mr. Manigodjic, and I'll come back to this story, did Zejnil Delalic, both by his own example and by financial means, improve the standards of living in an area such as Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps, because we all lived in impoverished conditions after the war. I think that Zejnil Delalic was the first who sort of made good, and he achieved success. Then he started to support his home area, and he did so through either financial means or through advice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We're still talking about Mr. Zejnil Delalic before the war. How would you describe Mr. Delalic? What kind of a man was he?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: This friendship between us, as I said, it has been going on for the last 30 years. We had a lot of very fine moments over the course of this time. We would have long parties. After this period of 30 years, I felt that this person continued to go down the same path or stayed on the same track. That is both with respect to his attitude towards other people, with respect to his preparedness to assist people as much as he could. Even after this disaster which has visited us, I have not changed my opinion of him, because no detail from all this time we've spent together is pointing me in any other direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you know Miso Maric, a poet of Serbian ethnic background, and I'm telling you this because now it's become necessary for us to introduce ourselves in ethnic terms as well, and also a member of the rock group Indexe called Pimpek?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do know these people, and I saw those two persons at Zejnil Delalic's, especially, Miso Maric. These two persons were more involved in entertainment, but there were also other people who were involved in political life. This was a home where everybody liked to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During this entire period in which you knew Mr. Delalic before the war, and you said that you haven't changed your opinion about him since, did you ever notice any trace of nationalism with Mr. Delalic or certain narrow-mindedness with respect to a certain ethnic background of any person?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: No, I really did not -- I neither experienced it, nor ever felt it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Manigodjic, you spent the war in Jablanica. Did you have an opportunity to meet with Zejnil Delalic, and did you ever feel that his attitude towards you and members of other ethnic communities, did you ever feel that he changed his attitude towards you and his other friends, in any way?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I did meet on two or three occasions with Zejnil Delalic in Jablanica. This was after the war had begun. This was not part of any organised get-together. I just came across him because we had other duties at the time. We did not have, of course, much time left for socialising at that time. However, I really could not notice any change in his attitude, any change in our relationship, anything that I would qualify as a changed type of behaviour, anything that would be termed as some kind of nationalism. No, really, nothing was changed between the two of us. I don't think he ever changed his attitude towards others either.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You say that you used to meet him, you used to see him in the company of people coming from various walks of life, people who were engaged in politics, entertainment, sports, and so on. Did Delalic treat every one of you equally, as his friends, as his acquaintances, or did he ever try to teach anyone any lessons?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: See, we did get together very frequently, and we would discuss things. We tried to be active in social terms. We organised a number of good actions, and Zejnil was involved in that. We were all involved in that, his friends, myself. No, he never looked down on anyone. He never put his own finger in it. He always treated us equally. I'm sure that he was in a position to help more than it was the case with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I had said that I would go back to one thing that you mentioned earlier on in your testimony. However, I have one question prior to that. When you left Jablanica, where did you go and did you subsequently meet with Mr. Zejnil Delalic? When was it, after the war, that you left Jablanica? Where did you go, and did you see Zejnil Delalic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the war, I left the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina for the first time. It was in April 1995. I went to see my relatives in Germany, and I was passing through Vienna where I had lots of friends, a lot of people I knew from Jablanica. I had some regards to convey, and I stopped at the club of friends of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Vienna. I did not wish to stay longer than one day, but then again, it was the old Zejnil that I came across, the same old Zejnil as he was before the war, so I stayed for three or four days, and I had a very good time with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have testified about his being friendly and helpful to everybody, regardless of their nationality. Did you experience the same kind of attitude towards you, yourself, and other people in Vienna on the occasion when you met him there?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, absolutely. He was the same. He had the same attitudes towards everyone else. He was treating us like a gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There is one more area, and it is going to be the last area that I want to cover, something I would like to ask you, Mr. Manigodjic. You mentioned that you had an idea to organise exchange between two schools and that this was the result of the efforts of some businessmen, people who were working in Germany. Is it true that you provided me with certain letters from that school and press articles from 1981 which speak about the efforts put forth by Zejnil Delalic to organise something that amounted to an interstate cooperation between two groups of young people? Did you provide me with this from your own personal documentation?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is my personal property, and these articles refer to the exchange of schools. This is just a small detail which can be supported with a number of names of people who were involved in that exchange, something that can further explain how this cooperation went.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you were one of the organisers of these exchanges?

utterances.speaker: NEBOJSA MANIGODJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was also one of the organisers. I took part in the whole project from the beginning to the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would kindly ask the assistance of the usher to distribute this material, and I have already given this to the Prosecutor. We would like to tender this into evidence, because it goes to the activities of Zejnil Delalic in 1981 in a humanitarian area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can I have the numbers for identification, please? This would conclude the examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D202/1, D203/1, the first one being "Friendship on the Neretva River," and D203/1 being the school comprising the elementary, secondary and high schools, district of Offenbach.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are these documents admitted into evidence, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: These are earlier than the activities you're complaining about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I haven't received a translation of your comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The documents are so many years earlier than the activities we are talking about. Are there any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Does Your Honour wish me to start cross-examination now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You might start tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will now rise and reassemble at 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: 5.37 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 15th day of October, 1998 at 10.00 a.m.
